mappings.note: Asks for the reciprocal-sum rule for three resistors in parallel - the parallel half of LO-2 stated as a formula rather than evaluated.
Which combination lowers resistance. A one-step consequence of the parallel rule, so LO-2; no Ohm's law or material property is in play.
Names and defines the ampere from one coulomb per second. The definition of current has no outcome in this set - LO-1 treats current only as a term of V = IR. Content gap.
Voltmeter resistance justified by its parallel placement and the need to draw negligible current - meter behaviour under LO-5, not a resistance-of-a-conductor question.
Common PD across parallel branches. Paired with the series-current item as the defining property of the other combination; LO-2 is the only outcome that owns either.

Same current, different heat: LO-2 supplies H proportional to R at fixed I, LO-3 supplies why the thin filament has far greater resistance than the line wire. Both halves are needed for the explanation.
Ratio of resistances from rated powers via R = V^2/P, with a numerical factor demanded. Power rating is the input, so C 2.5-LO-1 rather than C 2.4-LO-1.

Disadvantages of series wiring - common current forcing unequal appliances to share it, and one failure breaking the whole loop. Both are properties of the series combination, so LO-2, argued qualitatively rather than computed.

General-awareness item about electricity as the convenient transmissible form of energy. No competency or outcome in the legal set covers it - C 2.5's outcomes need a power or energy value and C 2.4's need a circuit quantity - so it is pinned only at goal level. Poor fit.
Bare substitution R = V/I with a single pair of values. The simplest member of the numerical Ohm's law family, with no combination, geometry or power step.
Two equal resistors give 48 ohm in series and 12 ohm in parallel (LO-2), then P = V^2/R turns that into a 4:1 power ratio (C 2.5-LO-1). Neither step alone reaches the answer, so both are cited.
Current falls to one fourth when V does at constant R, and the law must be named. This is the 'states and uses' pairing of LO-1 in one item, with no numbers substituted.

Alloy heating elements in toasters and irons: LO-2 owns the heating devices, LO-3 owns the higher-resistivity-than-constituents argument. The oxidation reason has no outcome and rides along under 'material'.

Infers ohmic behaviour from a straight V-I line (LO-1) and then explicitly requires a labelled circuit diagram with ammeter and voltmeter to obtain it - the clearest LO-5 fit in the chapter, since both halves of that outcome are demanded.
Oven cord versus element - the same heat-goes-where-the-resistance-is argument as the bulb filament item, with LO-3 carrying the reason the two resistances differ.
Requires a drawn domestic circuit with standard symbols (LO-5) in which the fuse is the graded safety element (C 2.5-LO-2). Earthing, the other half of the answer, is named in no outcome.
Reads a milliammeter and a voltmeter scale, least count included (LO-5), then R = V/I from those readings (LO-1). The meter-reading step is graded separately here, which is why LO-5 leads.
Uses of electricity in daily life. Pure general awareness with nothing to calculate, relate or draw; no competency in the legal set reaches it, so it is recorded at goal level as a poor fit.

Zero error of an ammeter and voltmeter and how to correct readings for it. LO-5 is the only meter outcome, though note it speaks of predicting readings rather than correcting instrument error, so the fit is approximate.
Least count and scale reading of both meters, with no resistance asked for. Deliberately not paired with LO-1 - unlike the near-identical item above, this one stops at the readings.

States Ohm's law with its expression (LO-1) and then asks what shape the V-I plot takes and why. C 8.1 rather than LO-5 because the graded representation is a graph, which LO-5's wording (circuit diagrams and meters) does not cover.

States the law, then demands the experimental circuit - battery, rheostat, ammeter in series, voltmeter across - which is LO-5. The third part, whether Ohm's law always holds, concerns non-ohmic conductors and is outside every outcome here.
The three factors of H = I^2Rt plus a named application. Entirely within LO-2; no power, energy or unit conversion is asked, which is what keeps it off C 2.5-LO-1.
Two reasons for nichrome heating elements, one of which is explicitly high resistivity (LO-3) and the other its behaviour when red hot in a heater (LO-2).
Converts 17 divisions into a current using the ammeter's least count. The arithmetic is scale reading, not Ohm's law, so LO-5 alone; no resistance or voltage appears.
